statement: At a gravity level of 0.10 G, the model predicts flame extinction at a pressure of 0.12 atm.
span: At a gravity level of 0. I0 G, the model predicted extinction at 0.12 arm pressure, lower than the experiments indicated.

statement: There is no significant difference in oxygen concentration flammability thresholds between 1/8-in. diameter rods and 1/2-in. wide samples.
span: The information obtained so far indicates there is insignificant difference in the oxygen concentration flammability thresholds when comparing 1/8-in. dia rods with ½-in. wide samples.

statement: For Mylar at 10.2 psi in Martian gravity, the flame extinguishes when the oxygen concentration is 17%.
span: When the oxygen is decreased in another test to 17%, the flame goes out.

statement: For TA-301, a 6 in. sample length results in a 1 percent lower MOC compared to 7, 8, and 12 in. sample lengths.
span: For material TA-301, the sample length of 6 in. shows a one percent lower MOC than MOC at 7, 8, and 12 in. in Figure 2.

statement: The implementation of a double-rolled hem increases the MOC by 1 percent.
span: In combination, both of these factors allow the implementation of a double-rolled hem to increase MOC by one percent.

statement: The flame length fluctuated at a frequency of 1.4 Hz before stabilizing at 90 s.
span: Initially the flame length fluctuated at about 1.4 Hz before finally becoming more stable at about 90 s

statement: The average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s and the estimated average flame power is 1200 W.
span: Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W

statement: The flame length and brightness varied at a frequency of 1.4 Hz before stabilizing at 90 s.
span: At first, the flame length and brightness varied significantly at a periodic frequency of about 1.4 Hz before finally becoming more stable at about 90 s into the test.

statement: The average concurrent-flow flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s, while the opposed-flow flame average spread rate is 1.3 mm/s.
span: The average concurrent-flow flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s. The opposed-flow flame average spread rate 1.3 mm/s.

statement: The flame spread rate for a 5-cm-wide sample is 2.1 mm/s, which is faster than the 1.8 mm/s spread rate for a 40.6-cm-wide sample at a flow speed of 20 cm/s.
span: The flame spread rate for the 5-cm-wide sample is marginally faster compared to the spread rate for the 40.6-cm-wide sample for the same flow speed of 20 cm/s (2.1 compared to 1.8 mm/s).

statement: Nomex HT90-40 requires an oxygen concentration of 24 to 25% to burn on Earth.
span: On Earth, it will only burn if the oxygen concentration is increased to around 24 to 25%.

statement: Most of the data shows a CO to CO2 ratio well above 0.004, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.
span: As can be seen, most of our data is well above that, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.

statement: Clear trends are observed for CO2 generation relative to measured fuel mass loss.
span: There are clear trends observed for O2 consumption and CO2 generation relative to measured fuel mass loss.

statement: Clear trends are observed for oxygen consumption relative to measured fuel mass loss.
span: There are clear trends observed for O2 consumption and CO2 generation relative to measured fuel mass loss.

statement: The 7-g fuel mass loss test had over 1,000 ppm of CO.
span: The 7-g fuel mass loss test had over 1,000 ppm of CO (above the range of the sensor).

statement: CO generation generally increases with increasing fuel mass loss.
span: CO generation generally increases with increasing fuel mass loss and O2 consumption.

statement: CO generation generally increases with increasing oxygen consumption.
span: CO generation generally increases with increasing fuel mass loss and O2 consumption.

statement: At these thicknesses (100, 200, 300, and 400 μm), the fuel can be considered thermally thin because the maximum spread rate was found to be inversely proportional to fuel thickness, which is a hallmark of a thermally thin regime.
span: At all these thicknesses, the fuel can be considered thermally thin because the maximum spread rate was found to be inversely proportional to fuel thickness (Ref. 1), a hallmark of a thermally thin regime.

statement: Steady flame spread over thin fuels in a perfectly quiescent microgravity environment has been established at higher oxygen levels.
span: This result is also dependent on other ambient conditions as steady spread over thin fuels in a perfectly quiescent environment has been established at higher O2 levels (Ref. 11).

statement: The flame spread rate measurement result was found to be reproducible within 5% uncertainty regardless of how the flame movement was tracked.
span: The result has been found to be reproducible within 5 percent uncertainty regardless of how the flame movement is tracked.

statement: Flame spread over a 100-µm-thick PMMA sheet was observed 10 seconds after ignition under ambient conditions of 20.7% O2, 1 atm, and an opposed-flow velocity of 2.5 cm/s.
span: A typical color image of the top view 10 s after ignition is shown in Figure 2.7(a) for flame spread over 100-µm-thick PMMA sheet for the ambient conditions of 20.7 percent O2, 1 atm, and an opposed-flow velocity of 2.5 cm/s.

statement: The ignition wire was observed glowing red at x = 36 mm, and the burnout location was observed as a black line at x = 42 mm in the picture.
span: The ignition wire, glowing red at x = 36 mm, and the burnout location, the black line at x = 42 mm are visible in this picture.

statement: A flame propagating at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s over a 100-µm sample extinguished within 2 seconds when the flow was abruptly cut off.
span: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s.

statement: Downward flame spread experiments were performed at a pressure of 101 kPa and an oxygen concentration of 0.21.
span: The downward experiments were performed in the atmospheric condition (pressure 101 kPa, O2 level 21 percent).

statement: For downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit, the average flame spread rate is 0.044 mm/s.
span: Although for thicker fuels, the spread rate is slightly width dependent, a value of 0.042 mm/s for a 10-cm-wide sample (Ref. 23) as opposed to 0.044 mm/s for the 2-cm-wide sample, an average value of 0.044 mm/s is selected as the average spread rate for downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit.

statement: The transition thickness for downward flame spread in ambient air is 5.19 mm.
span: The transition thickness (2τtransition) can be calculated from this expression as 5.19 mm for downward flame spread in ambient air.

statement: The effective velocity induced by buoyancy for flame spread over thick PMMA is 1.9 cm/s.
span: With F evaluated, experimental data for flame spread over thick PMMA is used to determine the effective velocity induced by buoyancy as 1.9 cm/s.

statement: The transition thickness for PMMA in ambient air is 5.2 mm.
span: For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.

statement: For test M7, as the opposed-flow velocity decreased from 10 cm/s to 3 cm/s, the flame spread rate decreased from 0.106 mm/s to 0.07 mm/s.
For test M16, as the opposed-flow velocity decreased from 5 cm/s to 2 cm/s, the flame spread rate decreased from 0.144 mm/s to 0.1062 mm/s.
Higher flow velocity results in a higher flame spread rate.
span: As you see, the graph illustrates that the higher the flow velocity, or the thinner the sample, the higher the spread rate is.

statement: Thinner samples result in a higher flame spread rate.
span: As you see, the graph illustrates that the higher the flow velocity, or the thinner the sample, the higher the spread rate is.

statement: The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz.
span: The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz as shown in the inset to Figure 6.6, and drops to a value of 1.05 over a period of a few seconds followed by a large oscillation.

statement: The minimum flammability boundary occurs at 13.5 percent O2.
span: The minimum in this boundary occurs at a = 8 to 12 s–1 at approximately 13.5 percent O2, in good agreement with the predicted a at the minima in the flammability boundary (Refs. 6, 7, 20, and 21).

statement: On the blowoff side, decreasing oxygen concentration increases the flame standoff distance.
span: On the blowoff side, as O2 is reduced, the standoff distance increases.

statement: Reducing the stretch rate by two orders of magnitude results in a seven-fold increase in flame standoff distance.
span: The standoff distance shows a seven-fold increase as a is reduced by two orders of magnitude.

statement: On the quenching side, increasing oxygen concentration increases the flame standoff distance.
span: On the quenching side, as O2 increases, the standoff distance also increases.

statement: Flame spread rate decreases as flow velocity decreases.
span: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.

statement: Flame spread rate decreases as oxygen concentration decreases.
span: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.

statement: Flame spread rate decreases as sample width decreases.
span: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.

statement: Flame length decreases as flow speed decreases.
span: As the flow speed was reduced, both flame length and flame width dropped accordingly with flow.

statement: Flame width decreases as flow speed decreases.
span: As the flow speed was reduced, both flame length and flame width dropped accordingly with flow.

statement: The fire experiments produced heat release rates as high as 10 kW without causing average vehicle conditions to reach unacceptable levels.
span: However, despite having heat release rates up to 10 kW, the average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.

statement: Increasing the duct height slows the concurrent flame spread rate.
span: Since the concurrent flame spread rate increases with air velocity, increasing the duct height slowed the flame spread.

statement: Increasing the rib width decreases the flame spread rate.
span: The flame spread more rapidly on the thin ribs at the top of the image with decreasing spread rate as the ribs become wider .

statement: Increasing the ambient oxygen concentration increases the final length of the Saffire V-3 flame.
span: Increasing the ambient oxygen concentration can be expected to reduce the standoff distance. Consequently, the final length of the Saffire V-3 flame is greater than the other samples due to the enhanced oxygen concentration.

statement: In 0.254 oxygen, the PMMA sample flame grew to 11 cm after 450 seconds.
span: In Saffire V-3, the one-sided PMMA sample flame (in 25.4% oxygen) grew to 11 cm after 450 seconds.

statement: In the spacecraft, the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide was more significant than the rise in temperature and pressure.
span: Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.

statement: The fire intensity for the tests was between 1.5 kW and 3 kW.
span: The fires were generally of 1.5 to 3 kW in intensity which is a small fire by terrestrial standards.

statement: The Nomex sample failed to ignite.
span: The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper.
